newsitem.title: MEXICO: Femsa seen placing loan to replace bond.
newsitem.headline: Femsa seen placing loan to replace bond.

text.p: Mexican beverage company Fomento Economico Mexicano S.A. (Femsa) is expected to take out a syndicated loan worth $350 million and use the proceeds to replace its $300 million Eurobond, analysts said.
The move is part of Femsa's strategy to restructure its outstanding debt, they added.

The Monterrey-based company was intially seen replacing its five-year Eurobond that comes due this July with another bond, but analysts said the company has instead opted to take out a three-year syndicated loan.
That will allow the company to replace the Eurobond, which has a coupon of 9.5 percent, with cheaper debt.

Femsa could also liquidate the credit and reduce its leverage once it sells a minority stake in either its beer or packaging subsidiaries in secondary offerings, Valores Finamex analyst Francisco Rivero said.

"I assume this syndicated loan will continue at the corporate level and not at the subsidiary level, but eventually as they have the IPOs for the subsidiaries they will pay down debt at the corporate level," Rivero told Reuters.
The move continues a trend seen in Mexico of borrowers taking out syndicated loans instead of placing bonds, gaining with cheaper costs and the ease in taking out the loans.
A syndicated loan will also be easier to pay back than a Eurobond, and moreover, in the competitive Mexican loan market blue-chip Mexican companies can obtain very attractive terms, analysts said.
Femsa's unsecured loan will have a three-year term and a step-up interest rate of Libor plus 150 basis points in the first stage and then Libor plus 200 basis points in the second, Rivero said.
The loan is expected to be led by SBC Warburg, but sources said that J.P. Morgan and ING Barings have also come into the credit.
Femsa is Mexico's anchor bottler for Coca-Cola and the country's second largest brewer. It also has a packaging division and a national chain of retail stores.
Femsa has a strategy of eventually reducing debt at the holding company level, thus leaving each of its four subsidiaries with their own debt loads.
Analysts note that Femsa, at a holding company level, is aiming to become much more flexible and better able to participate in growth of the company.
"Eventually Femsa, as a holding company, will not only be debt free but will have cash in hand," said Bear Stearns analyst Carlos Laboy.
Analysts say that all of the subsidiaries could eventually be listed publically, following the lead of bottler Coca-Cola Femsa, which already trades.
Femsa's total debt, including that of subsidiaries, is $970 million, with the holding company having $440 million, analysts said.
Officials at Femsa were not available for comment.
